parsed_answer.content:
In the Spring Framework, `@RequestMapping` and `@GetMapping` are foundational annotations used to map web requests to specific handler methods within Spring MVC or Spring Boot controllers. `@RequestMapping` is the original, comprehensive mapping annotation introduced in early versions of Spring. It acts as a swiss-army knife, capable of handling any HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, etc.) depending on how its explicit `method` attribute is configured. Because of this broad applicability, it can be applied at both the class level to establish a shared URI prefix and the method level to target specific endpoints.

On the other hand, `@GetMapping` is a specialized, composed annotation introduced in Spring 4.3 to streamline and simplify code readability through meta-annotation. Under the hood, `@GetMapping` is simply a shortcut for `@RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.GET)`. It eliminates boilerplate configuration by hardcoding the HTTP method to GET, forcing developers to rely on dedicated annotations like `@PostMapping`, `@PutMapping`, or `@DeleteMapping` for mutating operations. Understanding the distinction between these two annotations is essential for building clean, maintainable RESTful APIs that adhere strictly to HTTP semantics and constraints.

items: Meta-annotation architecture: Spring processes composed annotations by scanning the hierarchy for annotations meta-annotated with @RequestMapping, registering the handler method with the exact sameDispatcherServlet mappings.
HTTP method safety: Using @GetMapping enforces safe and idempotent API design constraints, preventing accidental mapping of state-changing payloads to GET endpoints.

RequestMapping fallback attributes: When using general @RequestMapping at the method level without specifying a method type, Spring will route *all* HTTP verbs to that single handler, which frequently results in unexpected MethodNotAllowed or payload-binding bugs.

parsed_answer.content: A common production gotcha occurs when developers use class-level @RequestMapping alongside method-level annotations without specifying consumes or produces constraints. If multiple GET handlers match a URI pattern due to ambiguous path variables or overlapping ant-path expressions, Spring's RequestMappingHandlerMapping may throw an IllegalStateException during startup or dispatch unpredictable requests. Always prefer specialized annotations like @GetMapping over bare @RequestMapping to keep your URL space strictly typed and semantically sound.
